title: School Calendars Are a Choice
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman interviews Shana Young, a former state education agency leader and parent, about why school calendars in the D.C. area and elsewhere have become scattered with random days off, half days and snow days. Their shared argument is that large districts have stretched the same amount of instruction across more calendar days, which shifts real costs onto working families in lost wages, childcare and mental load. Young explains that half days still count as full days toward the 180-day mandate, so they function as a way to squeeze in teacher professional development without delivering a full day of learning. They acknowledge that religious holidays and community feedback drive some of the change, so parents share ownership of the result. The conversation closes on weather: districts that spend their slack on fall days off have to claw back snow days in June, when little real instruction happens. Their framing is that a calendar is always a set of choices, and a default is also a choice.
points: Districts have kept instructional time constant while spreading it across more days, so the visible cost of extra days off falls on parents who must cover childcare or forgo wages.
Mid-week days off that match no federal holiday are described as worse than long weekends because they align with no normal adult work schedule.
Half days count as full instructional days toward state mandates, which lets districts schedule PD and other priorities while delivering far less teaching than the calendar suggests.
Pluralistic communities and parent requests drive some calendar growth, so the interview treats parents as co-owners of the problem rather than only victims of it.
Planning for predictable winter weather, possibly with an emergency virtual option, would protect instruction better than making up snow days with half days and movies in June.
quotes: Many large districts in the D.C. area and around the country have stretched their school calendars across more days of the year, even as students receive the same amount of instruction. The difference is more days off scattered throughout the year for religious holidays, teacher professional development, and other breaks.
I support school leaders to reflect on how their policies and decisions reflect their values, and that even a default is a choice.

You mentioned having a lot of Mondays and Fridays off, but even worse are random Tuesdays and Thursdays or half-day Wednesdays, which are not aligned to federal holidays and not aligned to any normal adult schedules.
It can mean forgoing wages or using vacation days, and it’s essentially a financial tax on parents, not to mention the mental load of having to keep track of it all.

In most school districts, half days count for a full day of instruction toward the state’s 180-day mandate. So it’s a way for districts to squeeze in things that they think are important, like professional development for teachers, and still count it as a full day of school, even when kids are not getting a full day of instruction.
When we don’t plan, what ends up happening is that instruction is not made up in any meaningful way. Too many snow days can put kids and teachers behind.

The school calendar reflects a set of choices, not defaults, and we should be more intentional about those choices. We should make sure the calendar reflects our values, provides consistent instruction for kids, and follows a schedule that families can actually manage.
